issues.legal_issue: Misconduct directed against a fellow employee may be connected to employment even when the delinquent employee was not performing official duties at the time.
material_facts: The employer's security officer went to investigate a report of unauthorised construction on the employer's property while carrying out his property-protection duties.
The employee intervened, obstructed and threatened the officer, and physically handled him while the officer was investigating the report.
Both the employee and the officer were employees of the same concern.
issues.conclusion: The required connection with employment existed. Misconduct directed against a fellow employee who was discharging official duties may constitute misconduct even if the delinquent employee was not then performing official duties.
issues.legal_principle: A private quarrel between an employee and a stranger, with which the employer is unconcerned, ordinarily falls outside misconduct. But conduct subversive of workplace discipline, or misbehaviour directed against a fellow employee acting in the discharge of official duties, may constitute misconduct when both are employees of the same concern; the delinquent employee need not also be performing official duties. The Court distinguished Tata Oil Mills Co. Ltd. v. Its Workmen, [1964] 7 SCR 555, and W.M. Agnani v. Badri Das, [1963] 1 LLJ 684.

rule.if: disciplinary_misconduct_case and both_workers_employees_of_same_concern and conduct_directed_against_fellow_employee and target_acting_in_official_duties

predicates.disciplinary_misconduct_case: The employer has treated an employee's conduct as a ground for disciplinary action.
predicates.both_workers_employees_of_same_concern: The employee whose conduct is challenged and the person against whom it was directed both work for the same concern.
predicates.conduct_directed_against_fellow_employee: The employee's conduct was directed against the other employee.
predicates.target_acting_in_official_duties: The other employee was acting in the discharge of duties imposed by the employee's office.

issues.definition: When disciplinary misconduct is alleged, conduct directed against a fellow employee of the same concern while that employee is performing official duties can count as employment-related misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: An authority considering an employer's request to approve a dismissal during a pending industrial dispute has limited review jurisdiction, with different evidentiary scrutiny depending on whether the domestic inquiry was proper.
material_facts: The employer dismissed the employee while an industrial dispute was pending and sought approval of the dismissal.
The domestic inquiry was found to have been conducted in accordance with the applicable standing orders and natural justice, and its findings were supported by evidence.
The employer paid or offered the employee the required wages and applied for approval at the same time as the dismissal action.
The Court set out the inquiry to be undertaken both where the domestic inquiry is proper and where it is defective.
issues.conclusion: The authority's review is confined to the prescribed procedural, evidentiary, bona fide and statutory requirements. If the domestic inquiry is defective, the authority must assess the evidence itself; if dismissal is justified and the other requirements are met, approval is to be granted and relates back to the dismissal.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 33(2)(b) and its proviso of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the authority considers whether a proper domestic inquiry in accordance with the applicable rules or standing orders and natural justice was held; whether a prima facie case is supported by legal evidence; whether the employer reached a bona fide conclusion and the action is not unfair labour practice or victimisation; whether required wages were paid or offered; and whether approval was sought simultaneously or within a reasonably short time forming part of the same transaction. If the inquiry is defective, the authority assesses the evidence independently. Although punishment is generally for the management to determine, an unduly harsh, severe, unconscionable or shockingly disproportionate punishment may support an inference of mala fides. The Court relied on Lord Krishna Textile Mills v. Its Workmen, [1961] 3 SCR 204; P.H. Kalyani v. Air France, Calcutta, [1963] 1 LLJ 679; Central Bank of India Ltd. v. Shri Prakash Chand Jain, [1969] 1 SCR 735; Bengal Bhatdee Coal Co. v. Ram Probesh Singh, [1964] 1 SCR 709; Titaghur Paper Mills Co. Ltd. v. Ram Naresh Kumar, [1961] LLJ 511; Hind Construction & Engineering Co. Ltd. v. Their Workmen, [1965] 2 SCR 83; Workmen of Messrs Firestone Tyre & Rubber Company of India (P) Ltd. v. Management, [1973] 3 SCR 587; and Eastern Electric and Trading Co. v. Baldev Lal, [1975] Lab IC 1435.

rule.if: approval_proceeding_during_pending_dispute and ((proper_domestic_inquiry and prima_facie_case_supported_by_legal_evidence and bona_fide_nonvictimizing_dismissal) or (defective_domestic_inquiry and authority_independently_finds_dismissal_justified_on_evidence)) and required_wages_paid_or_offered and approval_application_made_promptly

predicates.approval_proceeding_during_pending_dispu: The employer seeks approval for a dismissal taken while an industrial dispute is pending.
predicates.proper_domestic_inquiry: The employer conducted the domestic inquiry in accordance with applicable workplace rules and the principles of natural justice.
predicates.prima_facie_case_supported_by_legal_evid: The inquiry evidence legally supports a prima facie case for dismissal.
predicates.bona_fide_nonvictimizing_dismissal: The employer reached its conclusion bona fide and the dismissal was not unfair labour practice or victimisation.
predicates.defective_domestic_inquiry: The domestic inquiry was affected by a defect or infirmity.
predicates.authority_independently_finds_dismissal_: After assessing the evidence itself, the authority finds that dismissal was justified.
predicates.required_wages_paid_or_offered: The employer paid or offered the employee the wages required in connection with the dismissal.
predicates.approval_application_made_promptly: The employer applied for approval simultaneously with the dismissal action or within a reasonably short time forming part of the same transaction.

issues.definition: In a pending-dispute approval proceeding, approval follows when the applicable inquiry and justification route is satisfied along with the wage and prompt-application conditions, and the approval takes effect from the dismissal.

issues.legal_issue: An approval authority exceeds its limited jurisdiction by refusing approval on an unsupported finding of no employment connection or victimisation when a valid inquiry and the other approval requirements support dismissal.
material_facts: The inquiry officers found that the employee obstructed, threatened and physically handled a security officer who was protecting the employer's property and investigating suspected unauthorised construction.

The Industrial Tribunal accepted that the inquiry was not biased, complied with natural justice and was based on evidence, but refused approval on the view that the incident lacked a rational connection to employment and was part of a civil dispute with hutment dwellers.
The employer paid the required wages and applied for approval at the same time as the dismissal action.
The Tribunal's conclusion of victimisation was based on conjecture rather than legal evidence.
issues.conclusion: The required employment connection existed, and the Tribunal exceeded its limited jurisdiction by withholding approval on the basis of conjecture and an unsupported reassessment. The High Court was right to set aside the Tribunal's order, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In an approval proceeding under section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the authority may not act as an appellate body where a proper domestic inquiry and supported findings establish a prima facie case. Once misconduct is properly found and the inquiry is not vitiated, victimisation or management bias cannot be inferred on the unsupported basis used here. The Court applied the limited-jurisdiction principles in Lord Krishna Textile Mills v. Its Workmen, [1961] 3 SCR 204; P.H. Kalyani v. Air France, Calcutta, [1963] 1 LLJ 679; and Central Bank of India Ltd. v. Shri Prakash Chand Jain, [1969] 1 SCR 735, among the authorities it discussed.
